We begin by rewriting $C$ in terms of $r$ and $\theta$ and noting that $$ C = \left[\begin{array}{rr} a \amp -b \\ b \amp a \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} r\cos\theta \amp -r\sin\theta \\ r\sin\theta \amp r\cos\theta \\ \end{array}\right] = \left[\begin{array}{rr} r \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp r \\ \end{array}\right] \left[\begin{array}{rr} \cos\theta \amp -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta \amp \cos\theta \\ \end{array}\right]. $$

Explain why $C$ has the geometric effect of rotating vectors by $\theta$ and scaling them by a factor of $r$.

Let's now consider the matrix $$ A = \left[\begin{array}{rr} -2 \amp 2 \\ -5 \amp 4 \\ \end{array}\right] $$ whose eigenvalues are $\lambda_1 = 1+i$ and $\lambda_2 = 1-i$. We will choose to focus on one of the eigenvalues $\lambda_1 = a+bi= 1+i. $

Form the matrix $C$ using these values of $a$ and $b$. Then rewrite the point $(a,b)$ in polar coordinates by identifying the values of $r$ and $\theta$. Explain the geometric effect of multiplying vectors by $C$.

Suppose that $P=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp 1 \\ 2 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right] $. Verify that $A = PCP^{-1}$.

Explain why $A^k = PC^kP^{-1}$.

We formed the matrix $C$ by choosing the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=1+i$. Suppose we had instead chosen $\lambda_2 = 1-i$. Form the matrix $C'$ and use polar coordinates to describe the geometric effect of $C'$.

Using the matrix $ P' = \left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp -1 \\ 2 \amp -1 \\ \end{array}\right] $, show that $A = P'C'P'^{-1}$.
